title: Stage I-A: Help Clients Tell Their Stories
overview: This chapter opens Stage I of Egan's problem-management model, which has three intermingled tasks: helping clients tell their story (I-A), find the real story (I-B) and focus on the right story (I-C). It explains why these tasks pervade all of helping, presents Stage I as collaborative client-focused assessment, and stresses linking it to action from the start. Focusing on Task I-A, it reviews research on client self-disclosure and illustrates storytelling through the case of Mara and Carlos. It then sets out guidelines framed by Hanna's precursors of change: working with all storytelling styles, starting where the client starts, assessing severity, clarifying key issues, exploring context, talking productively about the past, spotting unused opportunities and resources, and seeing problems as opportunities. It closes with helping clients move into action from the beginning, through proactivity and productive use of time between sessions, and summarises Stage I guidelines in Box 9.2.
objectives: Describe the three tasks of Stage I and explain why they pervade the entire helping process.
Explain client-focused assessment and the importance of linking Stage I to action early.
Summarise research on client self-disclosure and its relevance to Task I-A.
Explain and illustrate each guideline for helping clients tell their stories.
Apply Mehrabian and Reed's severity formula and discuss catastrophizing and ongoing assessment.
Evaluate the debate on exploring the past and describe three productive ways to discuss it.
Explain how helpers identify unused opportunities and resources.
Describe ways of helping clients act from the beginning, including between-session work.
Outline the guidelines for Stage I in Box 9.2.

sections.heading: A Brief Introduction to Stage I
sections.detailed:
People seek out helpers because they need help to manage their lives better. Egan opens Part III's first stage by explaining what Stage I is for: it is the stage in which counsellors help clients understand themselves, their problem situations and their unused opportunities, always with an eye to managing them more effectively.

Stage I is made up of three tasks, shown in Figure 9.1 (The Tasks of Stage I). Counsellors help clients (1) tell their stories (Task I-A, "The Story": what's going on?); (2) reframe those stories, develop new and more useful perspectives and start thinking about more constructive ways of acting (Task I-B, "The Real Story": what's really going on?); and (3) stay focused on the key issues and concerns that will actually make a difference in their lives (Task I-C, "The Right Story": what should I work on?). The figure sums up Stage I as helping clients explore concerns, get new perspectives, work on substantial issues and move to action, all feeding into ongoing action that leads to problem-managing outcomes.

Although the three tasks are described one at a time, Egan reminds the reader (as in Chapter 8) that in real sessions they are intermingled. The two-headed arrows linking A, B and C in Figure 9.1 make the point visually: helping does not move rigidly from the first task to the second to the third. A helper may move back and forth between storytelling, new perspectives and choosing what to work on within a single session.

This chapter deals with the first task, I-A; Tasks I-B and I-C are taken up in Chapter 10.
sections.simple: Stage I helps clients understand their problems and missed opportunities so they can manage them. It has three tasks: tell the story, find the real story through new perspectives, and pick the right story to work on. These tasks overlap in practice rather than following a strict order.
keyPoints: Stage I helps clients understand themselves, their problem situations and unused opportunities.
Task I-A: the story (what's going on?); I-B: the real story (what's really going on?); I-C: the right story (what should I work on?).
Figure 9.1 shows the three tasks linked by two-headed arrows.
The tasks are intermingled in actual sessions, not a rigid sequence.
Chapter 9 covers I-A; Chapter 10 covers I-B and I-C.

sections.heading: How the Tasks of Stage I Pervade the Entire Helping Process
sections.detailed:
Egan argues that the three Stage I tasks are not confined to the start of helping. He gives three reasons.

First, clients rarely tell the whole story at the outset. The full story tends to "leak out" gradually over the course of helping, so story-telling continues long after the first session.

Second, new perspectives are needed at every point in the helping process: while telling stories, choosing problem-managing goals, developing plans and implementing programmes. Blind spots can show up at any stage, so helping clients see things in a fresh, more useful way is always welcome, not just in Stage I.

Third, Egan stresses the word "right". The whole helping process is a search for what adds value for the client. Helpers can encourage clients to keep asking "right"-related questions throughout: Am I working on the right issues? Am I setting the right goals? Have I drawn up the right plan? Am I implementing it in the right way? Crucially, "right" means right for the client, not what suits the helper's favourite theory or preferred treatment approach. The client's test is whether it fits them, their resources and their personal culture. Clients remain the decision makers, but the helper can, and sometimes should, invite them to think through the implications of the decisions they are making.

The practical message is that I-A, I-B and I-C are recurring activities that run through Stages II, III and implementation, not boxes to be ticked once.
sections.simple: Stage I tasks keep happening throughout helping. Stories come out bit by bit, fresh perspectives are needed at every stage, and clients should keep asking whether they are working on what is right for them, not what suits the helper's theory.
keyPoints: Clients' full stories often 'leak out' over time.
New perspectives are needed at every stage; blind spots can appear anywhere.
Helping is a search for value; clients keep asking 'right'-related questions.
'Right' means right for the client (fit with self, resources, personal culture), not the helper's theory.
Clients decide, but helpers may invite them to consider implications of decisions.

sections.heading: Client-Focused Assessment
sections.detailed:
Stage I can be viewed as the assessment stage of helping (Hood & Johnson, 2007). Assessment here means finding out what is going wrong, which opportunities remain undeveloped and which resources are going unused.

Egan's version is client-centred assessment. It means helping clients to understand themselves, discover what is going on in their lives, notice what they have been ignoring and make sense of the messiness of their lives. Assessment in this sense is not something done to clients by an expert. It is a form of practical learning in which client and helper collaborate.

Egan acknowledges that other forms of assessment exist, such as psychological testing and the application of psychiatric diagnostic categories. These may or may not be useful, but he places them outside the scope of his book. The contrast is useful for exams: formal testing and diagnosis are helper-driven, whereas client-focused assessment is a joint learning process embedded in the client's own story-telling.

Later in the chapter (assessing severity) and in Box 9.2, Egan adds that assessment is ongoing rather than a one-time event at the start, because stories unfold over time.
sections.simple: Stage I can be seen as assessment: finding what's going wrong, what opportunities are missed and what resources are unused. For Egan this is a shared learning process between client and helper, not something the helper does to the client. Testing and diagnosis are outside his scope.
keyPoints: Stage I can be seen as the assessment stage (Hood & Johnson, 2007).
Assessment looks at what's going wrong, undeveloped opportunities and unused resources.
Client-centred assessment helps clients understand themselves and make sense of their lives.
It is collaborative practical learning, not something done to clients.
Psychological testing and psychiatric diagnosis are beyond the book's scope.

sections.heading: Linking to Action
sections.detailed:
Egan insists that the problem-management process should be linked to action early. Early gains signal that therapy is on the right track and is likely to succeed. What clients learn in Tasks A, B and C should be connected to the Action Arrow, and right from the beginning helpers should help clients act on what they are learning.

His illustration is Sal, a severely burned patient whose first response is to withdraw from people. In his despair Sal needs what Auerbach, Salick and Fine (2006) call "engagement": choosing to go on, finding some inner strength, being willing to reach out to people who care and can help, and being open to some way of dealing with the trauma whatever its size. Egan invites the reader to imagine sitting at Sal's bedside and to consider how they would help him open up and become active in his own helping.

The case shows that clients do not need "grand plans" before acting on their own behalf. Sal's therapist spoke with the burn centre's chaplain, who brought along a former patient. Sal opened up about his desperate thoughts; the recovered patient said he too had spent a lot of time chasing such demons away, and when Sal asked whether there was a way out, he told Sal that Sal himself was the way out. Sal asked if he could see him again and reached out to touch him. Telling part of his story to a stranger, asking for a return visit and reaching out were all actions, small ones, but hopefully the start of a flow. Sal was beginning to learn he could not make the journey alone, and that recovery would require many steps taken bit by bit, with formal and informal helpers supporting him.

Egan then returns to the structure of Stage I, the "current picture". Here counsellors help clients spell out their issues, concerns, difficulties or problems (he asks what Mara's would be). Each stage has three interrelated tasks, but they are not mechanical "now do this" steps. In Stage I they are activities that help clients state their concerns clearly, with neither too much nor too little detail. The three tasks help clients answer three questions: (1) What's going on in my life and what are my main concerns? (2) Looking more closely, what's really going on, and what new perspectives will help? (3) What should I be working on, and which issues, if handled well, will make a real difference?
sections.simple: Action should start early, because early gains show therapy is working. Sal, a burn patient, began acting in small ways (talking, asking for another visit, reaching out) without a big plan. Stage I tasks help clients answer: what's going on, what's really going on, and what should I work on?
keyPoints: Link problem management to action early; early gains predict success.
Connect learning from A, B and C to the Action Arrow from the start.
Sal's case: 'engagement' (Auerbach, Salick & Fine, 2006) means choosing to go on, inner strength, reaching out, openness.
Clients need no 'grand plans'; small actions can start a flow.
Stage I tasks are not mechanistic; they help clients spell out concerns with the right amount of detail.
Three questions: What's going on? What's really going on? What should I work on?

sections.heading: Task I-A: Help Clients Tell Their Stories
sections.detailed:
Task I-A is the first task of Stage I: helping clients tell their stories. Egan grounds it in research on self-disclosure.

Denise Sloan (2010) reviewed evidence linking self-disclosure in various settings, including psychotherapy, to psychological well-being. People generally want to talk about themselves both when life is going well and when it is going badly, and Sloan notes that besides strengthening social bonds, self-disclosure brings a wide range of health benefits. Egan finds it odd that there is more research on the benefits and dangers of therapist self-disclosure than on the pluses and minuses of client self-disclosure; perhaps, he suggests, the helping professions need to focus more on clients than on treatment modalities. The literature does discuss clients' "narratives", but that is a literary rather than a social-science term; most clients do not think in terms of life narratives, though they do have practical concerns about disclosing.

Egan stresses that helping clients tell their stories well should not be underestimated. Pennebaker (1995) observed that therapy lets people translate their experiences into words, and that the disclosure process itself may matter as much as any feedback the therapist gives.

While much has been written about clients' reluctance to talk, Farber, Berano and Capobianco (2004) describe the bright side of client self-disclosure. Most clients feel therapy is a safe place to disclose, made safer by a good therapeutic relationship. Disclosure at first produces shame and anticipatory anxiety, but eventually brings feelings of safety, pride and authenticity. Keeping secrets inhibits therapy, whereas disclosing brings relief from physical and emotional tension. Disclosures in therapy make later disclosures easier, both to the therapist and to family and friends. And clients feel therapists should actively pursue material that is hard to disclose.

On the other hand, fear of self-disclosure is a leading reason people do not seek therapy at all (Vogel & Wester, 2003). So helpers need to discern whether a particular client is eager to disclose or fearful of it. Farber and associates add that many clients not only need the helper's encouragement to talk about difficult issues but also welcome and appreciate it. Farber's (2006) book Self-Disclosure in Psychotherapy gives a comprehensive overview of both client and helper disclosure.
sections.simple: Task I-A means helping clients tell their stories. Research shows self-disclosure is linked to well-being and that putting experience into words is itself healing. Most clients find disclosure in therapy relieving after initial shame, but fear of disclosure also keeps some people from seeking help, so helpers must read each client.
keyPoints: Sloan (2010): self-disclosure is linked to psychological well-being and health benefits.
More research exists on therapist than on client self-disclosure.
Pennebaker (1995): translating experience into words may matter as much as therapist feedback.
Farber, Berano & Capobianco (2004): disclosure starts with shame/anxiety but ends in safety, pride, authenticity and relief.
Vogel & Wester (2003): fear of self-disclosure is a leading reason for not seeking therapy.
Helpers must discern whether a client is eager or fearful to disclose.

sections.heading: Mara and Carlos in Task I-A
sections.detailed:
Egan illustrates Task I-A with the continuing case of Mara and her counsellor Carlos (introduced in Chapter 4). Carlos knows that if he can help Mara get a reasonably clear picture of herself, her problems and her unused opportunities, she will have a better chance of acting on them. He uses the communication skills of Part II to help her tell her story.

Carlos opens with a simple invitation: what's going on and how can I help? Mara says she is not there to rehash her accident, though she is still working it through. She soon finds that talking about her broad dissatisfaction with the direction of her life is much more daunting than talking about the accident. She is not used to sharing concerns with anyone, even her parents, wonders whether she should have chosen a woman counsellor, and fears that talking to a stranger might "cause the dam to burst". Sensing this, Carlos suggests that some background about her and her family might help. That feels relatively safe, so her background emerges through the give and take of conversation.

Over that session and the next, Mara moves to more immediate concerns. She worries about her father, who has never recovered from the death of his son, the loss of his career or his self-imposed exile; his business is stagnating, he is increasingly dependent on her without admitting it, he neglects his health and may have had a mini-stroke. Mara also has her own issues: she feels she has stayed captive to "old country" cultural norms; young people she met in Iran seemed more culturally free and socially rich; she resents her cousins' materialism; she has been meeting a man from work for coffee without telling her parents, and feels guilty; and she has had insomnia and headaches for months while keeping up a good face. She reports all this in a very matter-of-fact way.

As she becomes more comfortable, Mara talks more freely, though with some hesitancy. Carlos recognises that stories do not tumble out in a neat package; they may "dribble out" across the whole relationship. He wonders whether to revisit the accident later, but Mara is in the driver's seat.

Egan draws a general lesson: clients differ radically in their ability to talk about themselves. Reluctance to disclose in sessions often reflects a wider inability to share oneself with others and to be reasonably assertive in everyday social life. Where that is so, one goal of counselling as a whole is to help clients develop the skills, confidence and courage to share themselves appropriately.
sections.simple: Carlos helps Mara tell her story by starting with safe background before she moves to harder concerns about her father, her culture, a secret relationship and her health. Stories come out gradually, and the client stays in charge. Reluctance to disclose in counselling may mirror difficulties sharing in everyday life.
keyPoints: Carlos aims to help Mara get a clear picture of herself, problems and unused opportunities.
Starting with family background gave Mara a safe way in.
Her concerns: her father's decline, cultural captivity, a secret relationship, guilt, insomnia and headaches.
Stories may 'dribble out' over the whole relationship; the client is in the driver's seat.
Reluctance to disclose may signal wider difficulty with sharing and assertiveness; building these can be a counselling goal.

sections.heading: Guidelines for Helping Clients Tell Their Stories
sections.detailed:
Egan introduces a set of guidelines for Task I-A, stressing that they are guidelines, not hard and fast rules. Some of the guidelines and examples involve the kind of "nudging" and invitations to self-challenge described in Chapter 6. Helpers must decide about such invitations on the basis of clients' needs, not their own theories: clients' needs take precedence over helping models.

As a frame for the guidelines, Egan presents Hanna's (2002) "precursors" of change, which together give a comprehensive picture of how people change and why they do not. This is Hanna's version of the readiness-for-change list from Chapter 8. On the client's part, the precursors are:
1. A sense of necessity ("I've got to do something about this").
2. A willingness to experience anxiety or difficulty.
3. Awareness of the main factors in the problem situation.
4. A desire to confront the problem.
5. Effort directed toward change.
6. Hope for a better future.
7. Social support.

Hanna calls these "regulators of change": the more of them a person has, the faster change will occur and, in some cases, the deeper it will go. As clients tell their stories, helpers can listen and probe for these regulators and even help clients develop them.

The guidelines that follow are: learn to work with all styles of storytelling; start where the client starts; assess the severity of the client's problems; help clients clarify key issues; help clients discuss the context of their concerns; help clients talk productively about the past; help clients spot unused opportunities; help them search for unused resources as they tell their stories; and help clients see every problem as an opportunity.
sections.simple: The guidelines are flexible, and clients' needs come before any helping model. Hanna's seven 'precursors' or 'regulators of change' (necessity, willingness to face anxiety, awareness, desire to confront, effort, hope, social support) speed and deepen change, and helpers can listen for and build them.
keyPoints: Guidelines, not rigid rules; clients' needs take precedence over helping models.
Some guidelines involve 'nudging' and invitations to self-challenge (Chapter 6).
Hanna (2002): seven precursors of change on the client's part.
Precursors: necessity, willingness to experience anxiety, awareness, desire to confront, effort, hope, social support.
As 'regulators of change', more precursors mean faster and sometimes deeper change.
Helpers can listen and probe for these and help clients develop them.

sections.heading: Learn to Work with All Styles of Storytelling
sections.detailed:
Both individual and cultural differences affect how willing clients are to talk about themselves, and therefore how they tell their stories.

Martina, 27, is highly verbal and eager. Her story pours out in rich detail, so the helper uses attending, listening, sharing highlights and probing only sparingly. Trained as a nurse, she works in her uncle's business, earns well but feels guilty because service matters to her, and feels hemmed in; a year in Europe whetted her appetite for adventure and she feels far from her great expectations. She has never got along with her mother, feels she abandoned her much younger brother by moving out, and fears her mother will smother him. Her partner of three years wants to marry, but she does not feel ready. She skips from topic to topic and finally laughs at how much she has said. From her story the helper learns she is young, bright, verbal and resourceful, eager and impatient, partly the author of her own problems, has blind spots, and has many unexplored options and opportunities. The counsellor even suspects she would make her way in life, however erratically, without counselling.

Nick is the opposite. Referred by a doctor because of trouble with his 9-year-old son, divorced about two years and living in a housing project on public assistance, he sits silently and will not look up. The counsellor uses many probes; even empathy draws out little. Tears come at times; about his ex-wife he says only "good riddance". Slowly and painfully the story emerges: his son's "trouble", the boy's growing uncontrollability and Nick's helplessness. Martina's story is full of possibilities; Nick's mostly of limitations. They are at opposite ends of the scale in both content and style.

Egan lists the range of variation helpers will meet: voluntary versus sent clients; long, detailed versus short, stark stories; emotional versus cold telling, even of terrible events; single-issue stories (e.g., getting rid of headaches) versus multiple-issue stories; stories about the inner world (self-hate, depression, loneliness), the outer world (finances, work, relationships) or both; clients who tell the core story at once versus those who first tell a secondary story to test the helper; and clients who trust the helper simply because they are a helper versus those who mistrust for the same reason.

In every case the helper's job is to build a working relationship and help the client tell the story as a prelude to managing problems and seizing the opportunities buried in it. A story brought into the open is the starting point for constructive change, and often airing it is itself a solid first step.

With clients like Martina, the helper may let them run on or insist on dialogue. If the whole story pours out nonstop, the helper cannot share highlights for every issue, but can help the client review the most salient points in an orderly way (e.g., "You've said quite a bit. Let's see if I've understood the main points..."). Such highlights show the client the helper has been listening intently and cares. Clients like Nick, who lack storytelling skills or are reluctant, are a different challenge; dialogue with them can be hard work.
sections.simple: Clients tell stories in very different ways. Martina pours out a rich, many-sided story; Nick barely speaks. Helpers must adapt: summarise the main points for talkative clients and use more probes and patience for reluctant ones, always aiming to get the story into the open.
keyPoints: Individual and cultural differences shape willingness to tell one's story.
Martina: verbal, eager, multiple issues, story full of possibilities; helper uses skills sparingly.
Nick: silent, reluctant, story mainly of limitations; helper uses many probes.
Stories vary: voluntary/sent, long/short, emotional/cold, single/multiple issue, inner/outer world, core/secondary, trusting/mistrustful.
The helper builds a working relationship; airing the story is often a solid first step.
For nonstop talkers, summarise salient points in order; reluctant clients need hard dialogue work.

sections.heading: Start Where the Client Starts
sections.detailed:
Clients begin their stories at different points, and they can start at any stage of the helping process. The helper's job is to join them there. "Story" is therefore used in its widest sense, not only as an account of what happened, how the client reacted and how they now feel. Helpers must stay with clients where they are, not where the helper would like them to be. This requires an intimate understanding of the "geography" of helping shown in the book's graphics: know where the client is before helping them think about where they need to go.

Egan gives five starting points:

Stage I: Exploring the problem situation. Norman returns to therapy after being fired. Last time he was taking drugs, belligerent at work and had lost a girlfriend. He has since got clean, which was hard, and expected that to sort things out. He worked successfully on a problem, but not the key one, which is probably relating to people. The helper can help him start over.

Stage II: Setting goals. Thad cannot decide between becoming a doctor or a politician (or political scientist) and must choose college courses this year. He faces an approach-approach conflict: he wants both goals. The helper can help him weigh the pros and cons of each.

Stage III: Choosing a course of action. Kimberley, a human resources executive, has learned that her chief executive, due to retire in six months, has behaved unethically. She is torn between exposing him, which could harm the company's reputation, and quietly monitoring him, which lets him get away with it. Her starting point is a dilemma about strategy; the helper can help her search for the strategy that best fits the institution's needs.

Implementation: The Action Arrow. Owen has committed to restraining himself when a neighbour does something "stupid", knowing that "speaking up" (flying off the handle) makes things worse, but he struggles because others act too slowly. His starting point is difficulty implementing a chosen course of action; the helper can help him find incentives to stick to his programme.

A failed solution. Martha kept tight reins on her teenage son as planned, but the more she controlled him the worse he became. She has gone through the whole helping process on her own and come up empty-handed. Her failed solution has created a new problem; the helper can help her look again at her son's behaviour and find solutions that fit both their needs.
sections.simple: Clients can begin at any point in the helping process, so helpers should meet them there rather than forcing a set starting point. Egan's examples show clients starting with problem exploration, goal choice, strategy choice, implementation trouble or a failed solution.
keyPoints: Clients can start at any stage; the helper joins them there.
'Story' is used in the widest sense.
Know the 'geography' of helping: where the client is before where they need to go.
Norman (Stage I): solved the drug problem but not the key problem of relating to people.
Thad (Stage II): approach-approach conflict; Kimberley (Stage III): strategy dilemma.
Owen (implementation): trouble sticking to a plan; Martha: a failed solution that spawned a new problem.

sections.heading: Assess the Severity of the Client's Problems
sections.detailed:
Clients bring problems of every degree of severity. Egan recommends James Hicks's (2005) award-winning book, written in clear language, on the most common signs of mental illness, a service most abnormal psychology books do not provide.

Objective versus subjective severity. Objectively, problems range from trivial to life-threatening. Subjectively, a client may experience even a minor problem as severe, and if the client thinks a problem is critical, it is critical for them. In such cases the client's tendency to "catastrophize", that is, to judge a problem as more severe than it is, becomes an important part of the problem itself. The counsellor's task is then to help the client put the problem in perspective or learn to distinguish degrees of severity.

Howard's life-story view. Howard (1991) observed that, as clients tell the story of a problem, they give the therapist a rough idea of their orientation to life, plans, goals and ambitions, and of the events and pressures surrounding the presenting problem. Over time the therapist must judge whether the problem is a minor deviation from an otherwise healthy life story, a normal developmental adjustment issue, or a sign of more fundamental trouble. If the former, therapy plays a minor supportive role and the life's major themes stay largely unchanged. If the life story's trajectory is fundamentally problematic, more serious, long-term story repair may be needed. Part of therapy can thus be seen as life-story elaboration, adjustment or repair.

Limits of helping. Savvy therapists grasp not only the severity of a problem and the extent of unused resources but also the limits of helping. They ask what the client's highest lifetime level of functioning has been and what expectations are therefore appropriate. Life-story adjustment or repair is not the same as trying to redo a client's personality.

Mehrabian and Reed's formula. Mehrabian and Reed (1969) proposed a still-useful, non-mathematical formula: Severity = Distress x Uncontrollability x Frequency. The multiplication signs show the factors are not merely additive: even low-level anxiety, if uncontrollable or persistent, can be a severe problem that badly damages quality of life.

Risk of harm. Sometimes helpers must assess for possible self-harm or harm to others. The suicide literature describes warning signs of self-harm, and the literature on violence in social relationships describes signs of impending aggression. Accounts of social violence, such as fired employees shooting superiors and colleagues, show how easily signs are missed.

Early warning tools. Cannon and associates (2008) developed a "new tool" for predicting, and so possibly preventing, psychosis in high-risk youth. A package of factors (a close relative with a psychotic disorder, problems functioning in daily life, unusual thoughts or suspicions, growing social difficulty and a history of substance abuse) predicted a 35% to 80% likelihood of an episode of losing touch with reality within 30 months. Other medical professionals did not regard this as a breakthrough and called for brain scans and genetic tests.

Because stories unfold over time, assessment is ongoing, not a one-time intervention at the start.
sections.simple: Problems vary from trivial to life-threatening, and what feels critical to the client is critical for them. Severity can be thought of as distress times uncontrollability times frequency. Helpers should watch for risk of harm, know the limits of helping, and keep assessing as the story unfolds.
keyPoints: Objective severity ranges from inconsequential to life-threatening; subjective severity is what counts for the client.
Catastrophizing (judging a problem worse than it is) becomes part of the problem.
Howard (1991): therapy as life-story elaboration, adjustment or repair.
Know the limits of helping: highest lifetime functioning sets expectations; repair is not redoing personality.
Mehrabian & Reed (1969): Severity = Distress x Uncontrollability x Frequency (multiplicative).
Assess for self-harm and harm to others; Cannon et al. (2008) psychosis prediction; assessment is ongoing.

sections.heading: Help Clients Clarify Key Issues
sections.detailed:
To clarify means to discuss problem situations and unused opportunities as concretely as possible, including future possibilities, goals, strategies, plans, implementation issues and feelings about all of these. Vagueness and ambiguity lead nowhere. Clarity means helping clients move from the general to the specific: specific experiences, thoughts, behaviours, intentions, points of view and decisions.

Janice. Janice's husband John has been severely depressed for over a year. After she faints, she sees a counsellor. Feeling guilty, she is hesitant to discuss her own concerns and says only that her social life is "a bit restricted" by his illness. Through empathic highlights and probes, the vague phrase gradually becomes a much fuller story (Egan gives a summary; she did not say it all at once). John has an undiagnosed fatigue-type illness. Janice swings between guilt, anger, indifference, hope and despair. She has no social life because friends avoid them, and she stays home because she feels she should not leave him. He is always tired, so they barely interact; she feels like a prisoner in her home. She sometimes cannot sleep, absorbs his hopelessness, believes a stronger or smarter woman would cope, hides all this from John and visitors, and feels as alone as he is.

This fuller story is told in specific experiences, thoughts, behaviours and feelings. Egan notes that Janice's own actions, staying at home and covering up her feelings, are part of the problem, not the solution. Now that the story is in the open, something can be done about it.

The law student with bulimia. A woman under psychiatric care for bulimia says she acted "a little erratically at times" with classmates. With highlights and probes, the fuller picture emerges: she sees herself as plain, has preferred going it alone since adolescence to avoid rejection, fantasised about classmates she thought would ignore her, imagined meals and sex with them, then purged to get rid of the fat and the guilt. She would seek out her latest imagined partner and then be rude to him to "get back at him". She was not truly delusional, but her external behaviour, through a twisted logic, reinforced her internal fantasies. Once her story became "public", that is, discussed openly with her helper, she began to take back control of her life.

The general lesson: vague labels such as "a bit restricted" or "a little erratic" conceal concrete patterns. Helping clients spell these out is what makes change possible.
sections.simple: Clarifying means moving clients from vague, general statements to specific experiences, thoughts, behaviours and feelings. Janice's 'a bit restricted' and the law student's 'a little erratic' turned into detailed stories once the helper used highlights and probes, and that openness made change possible.
keyPoints: Clarify = discuss problems and opportunities as concretely as possible.
Vagueness and ambiguity lead nowhere; move from general to specific.
Janice: 'a bit restricted' became a detailed story of isolation and roller-coaster emotions.
Janice's own actions (staying home, covering up) were part of the problem.
Law student with bulimia: 'a little erratic' revealed fantasy, purging and rudeness; going public helped her regain control.

sections.heading: Help Clients Discuss the Context of Their Concerns
sections.detailed:
Sometimes exploring the background or context of a concern helps clarify it. Egan calls this a further application of the people-in-systems approach to listening (Conyne & Cook, 2004; Cook, 2012; Egan & Cowan, 1979; Hutchison, 2003).

Tarik, in a management development seminar, tells his counsellor that he is a manager in a global consulting firm's Southeast Asian office. He is overworked, his new boss wants him on several time-consuming committees, and a subordinate (himself a manager) is undermining his authority. On the surface this is a "garden-variety" story found all over the world.

The counsellor, a Canadian, suspects there is more. He wants to understand Tarik's Middle Eastern culture to get the full picture; he knows there is a layer of Western culture in such firms but wants to deal with Tarik as a whole person. Through sharing highlights and a few probes, the background emerges. Tarik is not just a manager but a newly minted partner. The firm's structure is flat but its culture hierarchical, so he has been given the region's least desirable clients. His American boss has been there only four months, is rumoured to be staying just one more year as a pre-retirement "fling" in Asia, and is decent but distant and unhelpful. Tarik therefore sees his real boss as his boss's boss, whom company and cultural protocol prevent him from approaching. The troublesome subordinate is a long-standing but not very successful partner who thought he should have been given Tarik's unit and has been quietly sabotaging him.

A search for background quickly lifts the story out of the routine category. Egan cautions, however, that helpers should not seek background for its own sake. The right kind and amount of background provides both richness and context.
sections.simple: Exploring the background of a concern can transform a routine-sounding story. Tarik's work complaints took on new meaning once his counsellor learned about his culture, his status as a new partner, his distant boss and a resentful colleague. Background should be sought for richness and context, not for its own sake.
keyPoints: Exploring context is an application of the people-in-systems approach to listening.
Tarik's story first seemed 'garden-variety'.
The Canadian counsellor sought to understand Tarik's culture and treat him as a full person.
Background revealed hierarchy, a distant boss and a sabotaging rival partner.
Don't search for background for its own sake; the right kind and amount gives richness and context.

sections.heading: Help Clients Talk Productively About the Past: The Debate
sections.detailed:
Some schools of psychology hold that problem situations cannot be fully understood until their historic roots are uncovered, so their helpers spend much time exploring the past. Egan grants that if client and helper are "on the same page" about this, therapy can succeed. Others disagree. Glasser (2000) argued that although many people have been traumatised, they are not victims of their past unless they currently choose to be, and that solutions are rarely found in the past unless the focus is on past successes.

Fish (1995) suggested that searching for hidden root causes of current problem behaviour may be unnecessary, misguided or even counterproductive; constructive change does not depend on past causal connections. Egan sees evidence for this. Long ago Deutsch (1954) noted that even in carefully controlled laboratory conditions it is often almost impossible to establish whether event B, which follows event A, was actually caused by A. Linking complicated present behaviour patterns to complicated past events is an exercise in frustration.

Egan therefore gives three reasons why asking clients to find causal links between current unproductive behaviour and past events may be futile:
1. Causal connections cannot be proved; they remain hypothetical.
2. There is little evidence that understanding past behaviour changes present behaviour.
3. Talking about the past tends to focus on what happened to clients (their experiences) rather than on what they did about it (their thoughts, intentions, decisions and behaviours), and so interferes with the "bias toward action" clients need for managing current problems.

This does not mean the past has no influence or should never be discussed. Being stuck in the past is often a matter of rejection and resentment. But the fact that past experiences may influence present behaviour does not mean they determine it. Kagan (1996) challenged what may be called the "scarred for life" assumption: if orphans who spent their early years in a Nazi concentration camp can become productive adults, and young children made homeless by war can learn adaptive strategies after adoption by nurturing families, there is hope for everyone.

Egan admits this is an issue the helping professions argue about endlessly and that it cannot be settled in a few words. He then offers suggestions for talking about the past meaningfully and productively.
sections.simple: Some approaches dig deeply into the past, but Egan, citing Glasser, Fish, Deutsch and Kagan, argues that hunting for past causes is often futile: causes can't be proved, insight rarely changes behaviour, and past-talk can block action. The past influences but does not determine the present.
keyPoints: Some schools see current problems as understandable only through historic roots.
Glasser (2000): we are not victims of the past unless we choose to be; focus on past successes.
Fish (1995): searching for root causes may be unnecessary, misguided or counterproductive.
Deutsch (1954): even in the lab, causation between sequential events is hard to establish.
Three reasons causal past-talk may be futile: unprovable, little evidence insight changes behaviour, undermines bias toward action.
Kagan (1996) challenged the 'scarred for life' assumption: the past influences but doesn't determine.

sections.heading: Three Productive Ways to Talk About the Past
sections.detailed:
Egan suggests three purposes for which discussing the past is productive.

1. Talk about the past to make sense of the present. Many clients expect or want to talk about the past, and some ways of doing so illuminate the present, but the present must stay centre stage. How the past is discussed matters more than whether it is. In Egan's example, a man discussing how his interpersonal style gets him into trouble realises, with the helper, that his late father's cruel style lives on in him in smaller ways: his father beat his brother, whereas he cuts his brother down verbally; his father dictated to his mother, whereas he pushes "reasonable" proposals on her without listening. When the helper asks "But now what?", the client says he wants to change, recognising these as bad habits rather than something genetic. Egan notes that whether the father "caused" this does not matter; indeed, if linking the present to the past makes the client feel his nasty style is not his fault, that creates a new problem. Helping is about the future. Once the problem is named and in the open, something can be done. Very often problem situations have more to do with "bad habits" (Duhigg, 2012) than with sociobiological determinism.

2. Talk about the past to be reconciled to or liberated from it. A dangerous logic can underlie past-talk: I am what I am because of my past; I cannot change my past; so how can I change today? A client who began to dislike himself at 13 and got "locked into" believing life gets worse is not using liberation talk; the past still casts its spell. Helpers should understand that clients may see themselves as prisoners of the past, but, in the spirit of Kagan, help them challenge such self-defeating beliefs. By contrast, a father whose son was sexually abused by a church minister found he could not deal with his son's ordeal without revealing his own abuse by his father. After telling the whole story tearfully, he said in the next session that letting it out was like throwing off a dirty cloak of shame worn for years; painful, but now he felt different and good. That is liberation talk. Helpers should know their objective in discussing the past: to learn from it, or to be liberated from it? Expecting a "silver bullet" in the past to solve today's problems asks too much of it. King and Hicks (2007) showed that discussing lost opportunities and mistaken expectations, with their regrets, disappointments and humiliation, can be quite beneficial; people can learn and grow by reviewing what might have been, and recognising one's losses may even bring a paradoxical gratitude for loss itself.

3. Talk about the past to prepare for action in the future. Egan quotes historian A. J. Toynbee: history not used is nothing, because all intellectual life is action. Any discussion of problems or opportunities should lead to constructive action from Stage I through implementation, and insights from the past should stir clients to act. Christopher, realising how much his father and a high-school teacher had made him feel inadequate, resolved not to demean anyone around him, recognising that what he had called wit was actually meanness. Helpers should help clients invest the past proactively in the future.

Caveats. These guidelines are not set in stone, and do not mean clients may only talk about the past in approved ways. Short (2006) prefers not to focus on the past or symptoms but listens to such stories with respect and acceptance because people should not suffer alone. Doing otherwise would feed what Hansen (2005) calls the counselling profession's devaluation of clients' inner subjective experiences. Some approaches also make deeper exploration of the past essential. Recalling Chapter 1, in the hands of helpers competent in orchestrating the key ingredients of successful therapy, any solid treatment approach can be useful.
sections.simple: Talking about the past is useful when it helps clients make sense of the present, free themselves from the past, or prepare for future action. Helpers should know which purpose they are pursuing, avoid expecting a 'silver bullet' in the past, and still listen respectfully when clients need to tell past stories.
keyPoints: Make sense of the present: how the past is discussed matters more than whether; helping is about the future.
Problems are often more about 'bad habits' (Duhigg, 2012) than sociobiological determinism.
Be reconciled to or liberated from the past: contrast prisoner talk with 'liberation talk'.
King & Hicks (2007): reviewing regrets and lost opportunities can promote growth, even gratitude for loss.
Prepare for future action: Toynbee's 'history not used is nothing'; Christopher's resolve.
Caveats: Short (2006) listens with respect; Hansen (2005) warns against devaluing inner experience; any solid approach can work.

sections.heading: Help Clients Spot Unused Opportunities
sections.detailed:
Martina's story was about both problems and opportunities, and many stories mix the two. Early in modern psychology, William James remarked that few people use more than about 10% of their human potential on life's problems and challenges. Others have since said much the same, with different percentages, and few have challenged it. Egan suggests it is probably no exaggeration to call unused human potential a more serious social problem than emotional disorders, because it is more widespread. People with problems and relatively problem-free people alike have unused opportunities, so most clients will have opportunities that can help them manage their problems. Pursuing an opportunity can be a way of transcending a problem rather than "solving" it.

Bruno, 23, an accounting graduate student from a strongly religious background, said he was "obsessed" by sexual thoughts and felt guilty when he gave in to them. He valued his religion's emphasis on helping others, but studied accounting only for a decent job and found it unstimulating. Working in a bank and studying left little time for socialising or church volunteer work, which he planned to do "later". There was a vacuum in his life. Sensing an opportunity, the counsellor asked how far his church's focus on helping extended; Bruno said "to the whole world", then realised he knew little about the world. Developing a "sense of the world" made sense to him. The counsellor doubted that sexual obsession was the main issue. Bruno set up his own programme of reading, occasional lectures, a course in developing-country finance and the odd conference, made friends, met a like-minded young woman he began to date, and his "obsession" disappeared.

Clients talk about problems far more readily than about unused opportunities, which is a pity because many problems are better managed by developing opportunities than by tackling the problem directly. Lou Anne, a single woman in her mid-20s, was jailed for breaking into a government computer. In jail a friend, Marion, persuaded her to attend a religious service; the street-smart, "not too pious" minister impressed her, and when he learned she was a hacker he said they could really use her. After release she helped him set up a computer training programme for disadvantaged children, who listened to her because she had been a hacker, and she supported herself as a computer security consultant, which kept her up to date with hacking, still her passion. Egan remarks how fortunate it was that the minister saw talent, however misdirected, rather than depravity.

Box 9.1 (Opportunity Finding Questions for Clients) lists questions helpers can help clients ask themselves: What are my unused skills or resources? What are my natural talents? What resources are available in my environment? How could I use these to enhance my life? Which opportunities would help me transcend my problems? Which opportunities do I let go by? Which ambitions remain unfulfilled? What could I accomplish if I put my mind to it? Which opportunities should I be developing? Which role models could I emulate?
sections.simple: Most people use only a fraction of their potential, so almost every client has unused opportunities. Developing an opportunity can help a client rise above a problem rather than attack it head-on, as Bruno and Lou Anne show. Box 9.1 gives questions to help clients find these opportunities.
keyPoints: Stories usually mix problems and opportunities.
William James: most people use only about 10% of their potential.
Unused potential may be a more serious social problem than emotional disorders because it is more widespread.
Pursuing an opportunity can transcend rather than 'solve' a problem (Bruno, Lou Anne).
Clients talk more about problems than opportunities.
Box 9.1: opportunity-finding questions (unused skills, talents, environment, unfulfilled ambitions, role models).

sections.heading: As Clients Tell Their Stories, Help Them Begin to Search for Unused Resources
sections.detailed:
Incompetent helpers concentrate on clients' deficits. Skilled helpers do not ignore deficits, but they are quick to spot clients' resources, whether used, unused or even abused. These resources can become building blocks for the future.

Terry, in her late teens, is an involuntary or "mandated" client, arrested several times for street prostitution and now for drug possession. She ran away at 16 and was drawn into prostitution; she is street-smart and cynical about herself, her work and the world. Seeing counselling as a probation requirement and a game, she is hostile, insisting what she does is her own business and that counsellors are no better than people on the street, just more "respectable". The counsellor offers to talk about what is happening in the session itself rather than her life outside, and reflects her claim that no one could be interested in her; she retorts that she isn't even interested in herself. Terry has obvious deficits and a dangerous, self-defeating lifestyle. But the counsellor sees many resources: her toughness and street-smarts, and even the virulence of her cynicism and self-hate, the strength of her resistance and her near-unshakeable determination to go it alone. Many are currently used in self-defeating ways. They are misused resources, but resources nonetheless.

Helpers need a resource-oriented mind-set in all interactions. Egan contrasts two counsellors responding to a client who says he practically never stands up for his rights. Counsellor A, sticking to sharing highlights, reflects that "clamming up" is his policy and asks what happens when he speaks up; the client admits the world doesn't fall in and others sometimes listen, though he has little impact. Counsellor A then emphasises that speaking up doesn't get him much, missing the resource. Counsellor B notes that when he speaks up he is not blasted and even gets a hearing, then probes what makes him think he has little influence. The client realises that influence may not be the issue; he usually does not want to get involved. Both counsellors are empathic but focus on different parts of the message: A on the deficit, B on an asset plus a probe, producing a significant clarification. Not wanting to get involved now becomes the issue to explore.

The search for resources matters most when the story is bleak. Egan recounts a man who had suffered a bitter divorce, false accusations leading to dismissal, unemployment, serious health problems and homelessness, and showed only depression. When the helper reflected that he had been ground down, the man said "almost doing me in". The helper asked about the "almost"; the man said he was still alive and still talking. The helper observed this said something about his "fiber". The man looked up with a glimmer of something other than depression. The helper drew a line down a newsprint pad, listing life blows on the left and "Fiber" on the right, and together they added resources: musical talent, honesty, concern for and ability to talk to others. After about half an hour the man smiled, for the first time in months.
sections.simple: Skilled helpers look for clients' strengths, even misused ones, not just their weaknesses. Terry's toughness and stubbornness are resources being used badly. A resource-focused response (Counselor B) clarifies the problem better than a deficit-focused one (Counselor A), and spotting 'fiber' can lift even a very bleak story.
keyPoints: Incompetent helpers focus on deficits; skilled helpers spot resources (used, unused, abused).
Resources are building blocks for the future.
Terry (mandated client): cynicism, resistance and determination are misused resources.
Helpers need a resource-oriented mind-set in all interactions.
Counselor A highlights the deficit; Counselor B notes an asset and probes, clarifying the real issue.
Bleak stories: the 'fiber' exercise listed resources beside life blows and brought a smile.

sections.heading: Help Clients See Every Problem as an Opportunity
sections.detailed:
Clients come with a mixture of problems and opportunities. Egan cautions that pain should not be romanticised, but the flip side of a problem is an opportunity. His examples:
- Kevin used his AIDS diagnosis as a starting point for reintegrating into his extended family and challenging family members to face problems they had long denied.
- Beatrice used her divorce to develop a new approach to men based on mutuality, and, having to make her own way, discovered entrepreneurial skills and started an arts and crafts company.
- Jerome used a long convalescence after an accident to review and reset his values and life goals, visited other rehabilitation patients, found deep satisfaction, and began exploring the helping professions.
- Sheila used her incarceration for shoplifting, which she called "time out", to finish high school and get a head start on college.
- A couple mourning the death of their only child started a day-care centre with members of their church.

William C. Miller (1986) described one of the worst days of his life: projects failing, people unresponsive, workload growing. Later, over coffee, he headed a sheet "Lessons Learned and Relearned" and listed 27 lessons over seven pages. The day became one of the best of his life. He started a daily "Lessons Learned" journal, which helped him avoid self-blame and defeatism; on bad days he would tell himself the day would be full of learnings.

Egan concludes that helping a client spot even a small opportunity, whether the flip side of a problem or a standalone opportunity, can give enough leverage to put the client on a more constructive path.
sections.simple: Without glamorising pain, every problem has an opportunity on its other side. Kevin, Beatrice, Jerome, Sheila and a grieving couple all turned hardship into growth, and William C. Miller turned a terrible day into 27 lessons. Even a small opportunity can shift a client in a constructive direction.
keyPoints: Clients bring mixtures of problems and opportunities.
Don't romanticise pain, but the flip side of a problem is an opportunity.
Examples: Kevin (AIDS), Beatrice (divorce), Jerome (convalescence), Sheila (incarceration), a bereaved couple.
William C. Miller (1986): 'Lessons Learned and Relearned' list and daily journal.
A small opportunity can provide leverage for a more constructive course.

sections.heading: Help Clients Move into Action Right from the Beginning
sections.detailed:
Egan returns to one of the book's central themes. In Hamlet, Shakespeare speaks of "enterprises of great pith and moment" that lose "the name of action". Helping is such an enterprise, and it too can lose the name of action. One of the main reasons clients fail to manage their problem situations is their failure to act intelligently, forcefully and prudently in their own best interests.

Egan links this to positive psychology, whose strength is its focus on personal agency and self-regulation (Bandura, 2001; Caprara & Cervone, 2003). In Chapter 2 this was called a "bias toward action".

The practical implication is that action is not saved for the end of helping. From the very first session, helpers should help clients act on what they are learning. Two sub-guidelines follow: help clients see the importance of being proactive, and help them use the time between sessions productively.
sections.simple: Helping can become all talk and no action. Clients often struggle because they don't act wisely and firmly for themselves. Positive psychology's focus on agency and self-regulation supports Egan's 'bias toward action', so helpers should push for action from the start.
keyPoints: Hamlet: great enterprises can lose 'the name of action'; so can helping.
Clients often fail because they don't act intelligently, forcefully and prudently for themselves.
Positive psychology stresses personal agency and self-regulation (Bandura; Caprara & Cervone).
This is the 'bias toward action' from Chapter 2.
Two sub-guidelines: proactivity and productive use of time between sessions.

sections.heading: Help Clients See the Importance of Being Proactive
sections.detailed:
Inactivity can harm body, mind and spirit. A counsellor at a large manufacturing company realised that injured workers who stayed home tended to sit around, gain weight, lose muscle tone and develop psychological symptoms such as psychosomatic complaints unrelated to their injuries. Using a people-in-systems approach (Egan & Cowan, 1979), she worked with management, unions and doctors to create temporary, physically light jobs for injured workers, sometimes with nurses or physical therapists visiting them at work. Counselling sessions helped match the right worker to the right job. Active again, the workers felt better about themselves, and both they and the company benefited.

Egan observes that helping too often involves too much talk and too little action, and offers Marcus's case to show the almost magical effect of action. Marcus's "helpers" were his sister-in-law and a friend. Pushed into "retirement" from his office manager job because he supposedly did not fit a new e-commerce strategy, Marcus learned he had a cancer with an unpredictable course. Treatment left him tired, and he began having trouble walking for unknown reasons. A new marketing job had to be given up for health reasons. His daughter was expelled from high school for drug use and was sullen and indifferent; she and his wife clashed, and talks with his wife went nowhere. One of his married sons announced a divorce and a custody fight over a 3-year-old.

Though very independent and self-reliant, Marcus told himself he had to take charge of his life or it could fall apart, and that he could use help. He found it in Sarah, a savvy, no-nonsense sister-in-law who was a lay minister, and Sam, an old friend who was a family doctor. Sam helped him stay self-reliant by helping him research his illness online, without becoming preoccupied, so that he could partner with his doctors in choosing treatments. Marcus drew up a living will and gave Sam power of attorney to avoid needless prolonging of life. Sam also helped him pursue art, literature and theatre, interests he had never had time for.

With help from friends, Marcus used adversity as an opportunity to engage more fully with life, partly redefining life as good conversations with family and friends. Refusing to be a victim, he stayed active. He died two years later, but, in Egan's phrase, he managed to live until he died.
sections.simple: Being inactive harms people; staying active helps. Injured workers did better in light-duty jobs than sitting at home. Marcus, facing cancer and family crises, took charge with help from friends, stayed active and 'lived until he died'.
keyPoints: Inactivity harms body, mind and spirit.
Injured-workers programme: a people-in-systems approach (Egan & Cowan, 1979) created light jobs; workers and company benefited.
Helping often has too much talk and too little action.
Marcus faced job loss, cancer and family crises but chose to take charge.
Informal helpers Sarah and Sam supported his self-reliance, research, planning and interests.
Refusing to be a victim, he stayed active and 'managed to live until he died'.

sections.heading: Help Clients Use the Time Between Sessions Productively
sections.detailed:
If helping turns out to be short term for any reason, counsellors must help clients use the time between sessions as productively as possible. The helper's question becomes: how can I leverage what happens in the session to affect what the client does for the rest of the week (or month)? This does not deny the value of what happens in sessions; it capitalises on whatever learning or change takes place there.

Wosket's practice. Wosket (2006) ends each session by asking the client to describe what has happened and where they are, then asks whether there is anything they could do before the next session to move things along. At the start of the next session she asks what they did and what impact it had. If the client did nothing, she asks, without judgement, what they might have done if they had thought of acting. This reinforces the necessity-for-action theme.

Research on between-session work. Sixty-eight percent of practising psychologists frequently use between-session assignments (Kazantzis, Lampropoulos & Deane, 2005) to help clients act on what they learn in sessions (Detweiler-Bedell & Whisman, 2005; Kazantzis, 2000; Scheel, Hanson & Razzhavaikina, 2004; Tompkins, 2005; much of a 2002 issue of the Journal of Clinical Psychology was on homework). Daitch (2008) considers homework so important that she makes compliance part of the therapeutic contract, telling clients from the start about research showing that willingness to do homework is directly related to therapy's success. Mahrer and associates (1994) reviewed methods helpers use to influence clients to use between-session time productively. Broder (2000) offers many techniques for incorporating homework, discusses why some clients resist it and how to address resistance; with Albert Ellis, originator of Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy, he developed audiotapes on common client problems, which clients use to deepen what they learned in therapy and to work on resolving their conflicts.

The name versus the principle. There is no need to call between-session activity "homework". The word puts some clients off, strikes some helpers as too "teacherish", and can sound like an add-on rather than something flowing organically from sessions. The principle matters more than the label: use every stage and task of helping as a stimulus for problem-managing and opportunity-developing action. Use the term or "assign" tasks if that works for you and the client, but know clearly why you are assigning any task, and never assign homework routinely for its own sake.

Spontaneous action: Mildred. Homework often has a predetermined cast, but encouraging action can be spontaneous. Mildred, 70, a single retired teacher who had kept teaching past mandatory retirement until she was "eased out", was financially but not socially or emotionally ready for retirement. She became depressed and aimless and, at a friend's urging, saw a counsellor of about her own age. Knowing her internal resources had gone dormant, he told her in the second session that she was letting herself become a wreck, that she would never tolerate such behaviour from her students, that she needed to seize life again, and asked what she would do straight after the session. This "shock treatment" revived her; she asked what he did, they discussed what life offers after 70, and she decided her first task was to find a community, since school had been her community. She came to the next session with options.

Egan's conclusion: use homework or other, more organic ways of helping clients act. The helper's role demands being a catalyst for client action. Box 9.2 then summarises guidelines for this work.
sections.simple: Helpers should make sure clients use the time between sessions to act on what they learn. Wosket asks clients what they will do and follows up; most psychologists use homework, and research links homework to success. The label 'homework' is optional and should never be routine, and sometimes a spontaneous push (as with Mildred) works best.
keyPoints: Leverage in-session work to influence what clients do between sessions.
Wosket (2006): end-of-session review, plan between-session action, review next time, ask nonjudgmentally if nothing was done.
68% of practising psychologists frequently use between-session assignments (Kazantzis et al., 2005).
Daitch (2008) makes homework part of the contract; Mahrer (1994) and Broder (2000) on methods and resistance.
The principle matters more than the word 'homework'; never assign it routinely.
Mildred: a spontaneous challenge spurred action; the helper is a catalyst for client action.

sections.heading: Box 9.2: Guidelines for Stage I
sections.detailed:
Egan closes the chapter with Box 9.2, a summary of the main guidelines for Stage I work, organised under five headings.

Establish a working alliance: develop a collaborative working relationship; use the relationship as a vehicle for social-emotional re-education; do not do for clients what they can do for themselves, keeping the client in the driver's seat.

Help clients tell their stories: use a mix of tuning in, listening, empathy, probing and summarising to help clients tell their stories, share their views, discuss decisions and talk through what they want to do as concretely as possible; help them talk productively about the past; use probes when clients get stuck, wander or lack clarity; understand blocks to self-disclosure and support clients who find it hard to talk about themselves; invite clients to reframe their stories and develop new perspectives; and determine their willingness to engage in self-challenge.

Build ongoing client assessment into the helping process: get an initial feel for the severity of problems and clients' ability to handle them; note resources, especially unused ones, and help clients work with them; understand problems and opportunities in the larger context of clients' lives.

Help clients move to action: help clients develop an action orientation; help them spot early opportunities to change self-defeating behaviour or engage in opportunity-developing behaviour; find innovative forms of homework that help clients take problem-managing action in everyday life.

Establish a feedback and evaluation system: integrate feedback and evaluation into helping; get clients to participate in and own the evaluation process; keep an evaluative eye on the whole process, aiming to add value in every interaction and make each session better.

The box pulls together the chapter's threads: relationship, storytelling skills, ongoing assessment (severity, resources, context), action from the start, and evaluation.
sections.simple: Box 9.2 sums up Stage I under five headings: build a working alliance, help clients tell their stories, assess continuously, move clients to action, and set up feedback and evaluation.
keyPoints: Establish a working alliance; keep the client in the driver's seat.
Help clients tell their stories using tuning in, listening, empathy, probing and summarising.
Build ongoing assessment: severity, resources, larger life context.
Help clients move to action, including innovative homework.
Establish feedback and evaluation that clients participate in and own.

terms.definition: The first stage of the problem-management model, in which helpers help clients explore their concerns: tell their stories, find new perspectives and focus on key issues.
The first Stage I task: helping clients tell their stories; answers the question 'What's going on?'.
Helping clients reframe stories and develop new perspectives; answers 'What's really going on?'.
Helping clients focus on issues that will make a real difference; answers 'What should I work on?'.
What is right for the client, fitting their self, resources and personal culture, rather than what suits the helper's theory.
Collaborative practical learning in which clients come to understand themselves and make sense of their lives; not something done to them.
Connecting what clients learn in Stage I tasks to the Action Arrow from the very beginning of helping.
Choosing to go on, finding inner strength, reaching out to caring helpers and being open to dealing with trauma.
Clients revealing themselves and their concerns; linked to well-being and health benefits (Sloan, 2010).
A literary rather than social-science term for clients' life stories, used in the helping literature.
Client conditions that explain how people change: necessity, willingness to experience anxiety, awareness, desire to confront, effort, hope and social support.
Hanna's term for the precursors: the more present, the faster and sometimes deeper the change.
Stories that centre on one concern (e.g., headaches) versus several concerns, like Martina's.
Some clients tell their central story at once; others first tell a secondary story to test the helper's reactions.
Joining clients at whatever stage of the helping process they begin, rather than where the helper would like them to be.
An intimate understanding of the stages and tasks of the helping model so the helper knows where the client is.
Wanting two attractive but incompatible goals, as with Thad choosing between medicine and politics.
A starting point where a client's attempted solution has failed and spawned a new problem (Martha).
Judging a problem situation to be more severe than it actually is; it then becomes part of the problem.
Howard's view of therapy as working on a client's life story, from minor support to long-term repair.
Severity = Distress x Uncontrollability x Frequency; multiplicative, not additive.
Discussing problems and opportunities as concretely as possible, moving from general to specific experiences, thoughts, behaviours and decisions.
Listening to and working with clients in the context of the social systems around them.
The belief that early adversity determines later life; challenged by Kagan (1996).
A focus on what clients do about what happens to them; undermined by excessive past-talk; linked to agency and self-regulation.
