practice.answer: Catastrophizing is a client's tendency to judge a problem situation as more severe than it really is. Egan notes that if a client believes a problem is critical, it is critical for them, so the catastrophizing itself becomes part of the problem. The counsellor helps the client put the problem in perspective or learn to distinguish degrees of severity.

practice.q: State Mehrabian and Reed's formula for problem severity.
practice.answer: Mehrabian and Reed (1969) proposed: Severity = Distress x Uncontrollability x Frequency. It is not a true mathematical formula, but the multiplication signs show the factors interact rather than simply add up, so even low-level anxiety can be severe if it is uncontrollable or persistent.

Hanna (2002) listed client precursors of change: a sense of necessity, willingness to experience anxiety or difficulty, awareness of the main factors, desire to confront the problem, effort toward change, hope and social support. He calls them regulators because the more are present, the faster and sometimes deeper the change.

practice.q: What does Egan mean by 'liberation talk'?
practice.answer: Liberation talk is discussion of the past that frees a client from it rather than keeping them its prisoner. Egan contrasts a client still locked into a teenage belief that life gets worse with a father who, after revealing his own childhood abuse, felt he had thrown off a dirty cloak of shame.

practice.q: What is 'engagement' as described by Auerbach, Salick and Fine?
practice.answer: Engagement means choosing to go on, finding inner strength, being willing to reach out to people who care and can help, and being open to dealing with a trauma whatever its size. Egan uses it for Sal, a burn patient whose first reaction was to withdraw.

practice.q: Explain the three tasks of Stage I and why they pervade the entire helping process.
practice.answer:
Stage I helps clients understand themselves, their problem situations and unused opportunities so they can manage them better. Figure 9.1 shows three tasks. Task I-A, "the story", helps clients tell their stories and answers "What's going on?". Task I-B, "the real story", helps them reframe stories, gain new perspectives and think about more constructive action: "What's really going on?". Task I-C, "the right story", keeps them focused on issues that will make a real difference: "What should I work on?". Two-headed arrows show these are intermingled, not a rigid sequence, and Egan stresses they are activities, not mechanical steps; they help clients spell out concerns with neither too much nor too little detail.

The tasks are not confined to Stage I for three reasons. First, clients rarely tell everything at the start; the full story leaks out over time. Second, new perspectives are needed at every stage, from goal setting to planning and implementation, because blind spots can appear anywhere. Third, helping is a search for value, so clients should keep asking whether they are working on the right issues, setting the right goals, choosing the right plan and implementing it rightly. "Right" means right for the client and their resources and personal culture, not for the helper's theory. Clients make the decisions, though helpers may invite them to consider implications.

practice.q: Discuss research on client self-disclosure relevant to helping clients tell their stories.
practice.answer:
Egan grounds Task I-A in research on self-disclosure. Sloan (2010) reviewed evidence linking self-disclosure in many settings, including psychotherapy, to psychological well-being; people want to talk about themselves in good times and bad, and disclosure strengthens social bonds and brings health benefits. Egan notes, however, that more research exists on therapist self-disclosure than on client self-disclosure, suggesting the professions should focus more on clients than on treatment modalities.

Pennebaker (1995) argued that therapy allows people to translate experiences into words and that disclosure itself may be as important as any feedback from the therapist.

Farber, Berano and Capobianco (2004) described the bright side of disclosure: most clients find therapy a safe place, especially with a good relationship; disclosure initially brings shame and anticipatory anxiety but eventually feelings of safety, pride and authenticity; secrets inhibit therapy while disclosure relieves physical and emotional tension; disclosure in therapy eases later disclosure to the therapist, family and friends; and clients believe therapists should actively pursue difficult material. Many clients welcome the helper's encouragement.

Against this, Vogel and Wester (2003) showed that fear of self-disclosure is a leading reason people avoid therapy. The practical implication is that helpers must discern whether each client is eager or fearful to disclose and respond accordingly.

practice.q: 'Learn to work with all styles of storytelling.' Explain with reference to Martina and Nick.
practice.answer:
Individual and cultural differences affect how willing clients are to talk. Martina, 27, is verbal and eager; her multi-issue story about her job in her uncle's business, guilt over not serving others, conflict with her mother, worry about her young brother and uncertainty about marriage pours out in rich detail. The helper uses skills sparingly. She is bright and resourceful but impatient, has blind spots and many unexploited opportunities; her story is full of possibilities. Nick, referred because of trouble with his 9-year-old son, barely speaks; the counsellor uses many probes and the story of his son's uncontrollability and his own helplessness emerges slowly. His story is mainly about limitations.

Egan lists further variations: voluntary or sent clients; long or short stories; emotional or cold telling; single-issue or multiple-issue stories; inner-world, outer-world or mixed concerns; core stories told at once or secondary stories told first to test the helper; trust or mistrust of helpers. In all cases the helper builds a working relationship and helps the client bring the story into the open, often a solid first step to change.

With nonstop talkers the helper can help the client review salient points in order, which also shows they have been listening. With reluctant clients like Nick, dialogue is hard work.

practice.q: Describe the different starting points from which clients may begin their stories.
practice.answer:
Egan's guideline is to start where the client starts. Clients can begin at any stage of the helping process, so "story" is used in its widest sense, and helpers must know the "geography" of helping to locate the client before helping them move on. He gives five examples.

Stage I, exploring the problem: Norman, fired again, got off drugs but never tackled his key problem of relating to people; the helper helps him start over. Stage II, setting goals: Thad faces an approach-approach conflict between medicine and politics; the helper helps him weigh pros and cons. Stage III, choosing a course of action: Kimberley must decide whether to expose an unethical chief executive or monitor him until he retires; the helper helps her find the strategy that best fits the institution. Implementation, the Action Arrow: Owen struggles to stick to his resolve not to fly off the handle at neighbours; the helper helps him find incentives. A failed solution: Martha's tight control of her teenage son backfired and created a new problem; the helper helps her look again at his behaviour and find solutions fitting both their needs.

The point is to meet clients where they are rather than where the helper would like them to be.

practice.q: How should a helper assess the severity of a client's problems?
practice.answer:
Problems range objectively from inconsequential to life-threatening, but what matters is also subjective: if a client feels a problem is critical, it is critical for them. Catastrophizing then becomes part of the problem, and the helper helps the client put it in perspective.

Howard (1991) suggests that through the story the therapist judges whether the problem is a minor deviation from a healthy life story or a sign of deeper trouble, requiring supportive help or long-term life-story repair. Savvy helpers also know the limits of helping, considering the client's highest lifetime functioning; story repair is not redoing personality.

Mehrabian and Reed's formula, Severity = Distress x Uncontrollability x Frequency, shows that factors multiply, so even low-level anxiety can be severe if uncontrollable or persistent. Helpers may also need to assess for self-harm or harm to others, using the suicide and violence literatures, since signs are easily missed. Cannon et al. (2008) offered a tool predicting psychosis in high-risk youth, though other professionals questioned it. Because stories unfold, assessment is not a one-time event at the start but an ongoing part of helping, as Box 9.2 also stresses.

practice.q: How can helpers help clients find unused opportunities and resources?
practice.answer:
William James claimed few people use more than about 10% of their potential, and Egan suggests unused potential may be a bigger social problem than emotional disorders. Most clients therefore have opportunities that can help them transcend, not just solve, problems. Bruno's supposed sexual obsession faded once he developed a "sense of the world"; Lou Anne, a jailed hacker, turned her skills into teaching disadvantaged children. Since clients talk more about problems than opportunities, helpers can use the Box 9.1 questions: unused skills, natural talents, environmental resources, opportunities let go by, unfulfilled ambitions, role models.

Skilled helpers, unlike incompetent ones, look beyond deficits to resources that are used, unused or abused. Terry's toughness, cynicism and determination are misused resources. A resource-oriented mind-set shows in responses: Counselor A highlights the client's deficit, while Counselor B notes that he gets a hearing when he speaks and probes, uncovering the real issue of not wanting to get involved. With bleak stories this matters most. In the "fiber" example, a depressed man who had suffered divorce, dismissal, illness and homelessness admitted the blows had "almost" done him in; the helper picked up the "almost", named his fiber, and together they listed his resources beside the blows. For the first time in months he smiled.

practice.q: Discuss the guidelines for helping clients tell their stories.
practice.answer:
Introduction
Task I-A of Egan's problem-management model is helping clients tell their stories. Egan offers guidelines, not rigid rules, and insists that clients' needs take precedence over helping models. He frames them with Hanna's precursors of change: necessity, willingness to experience anxiety, awareness, desire to confront, effort, hope and social support. These are regulators of change, and helpers can listen for and develop them as clients talk.

Learn to work with all styles of storytelling
Clients differ widely. Martina pours out a multi-issue story full of possibilities; Nick barely speaks and tells a story of limitations. Stories may be long or short, emotional or cold, single- or multiple-issue, inner- or outer-world, core or secondary. Helpers build a working relationship, summarise salient points for nonstop talkers and work hard at dialogue with reluctant clients.

Start where the client starts
Clients may begin at any stage: exploring the problem (Norman), setting goals (Thad's approach-approach conflict), choosing a strategy (Kimberley), implementation (Owen) or a failed solution (Martha). Helpers join them there.

Assess the severity of problems
Severity is both objective and subjective; catastrophizing becomes part of the problem. Mehrabian and Reed's formula multiplies distress, uncontrollability and frequency. Howard sees therapy as life-story adjustment or repair, within the limits of helping. Helpers watch for risk of harm, and assessment is ongoing.

Clarify key issues and discuss context
Clarifying moves clients from vague to specific, as when Janice's "a bit restricted" became a detailed story of isolation. Exploring context through a people-in-systems approach turned Tarik's routine work complaint into a story of culture, hierarchy and sabotage, though background should not be sought for its own sake.

Talk productively about the past
Hunting for past causes is often futile (Glasser, Fish, Deutsch), and the past influences but does not determine the present (Kagan). The past is useful for making sense of the present, being liberated from it and preparing for action, while helpers still listen respectfully (Short, Hansen).

Spot unused opportunities and resources
Most people underuse their potential (William James). Opportunities can transcend problems (Bruno, Lou Anne), and Box 9.1 offers opportunity-finding questions. Skilled helpers spot resources, even misused ones like Terry's toughness, and respond like Counselor B rather than Counselor A.

See every problem as an opportunity
Without romanticising pain, problems have an opportunity side, as with Kevin, Beatrice, Jerome, Sheila and William C. Miller's "Lessons Learned".

Conclusion
Together these guidelines help clients tell their stories fully, concretely and in context, while keeping an eye on strengths, opportunities and action. They are applied flexibly: the helper adapts to the client's style and starting point, keeps assessing as the story unfolds, and treats the client as the decision maker. Underlying all of them is Egan's view that a story brought into the open is the starting point for constructive change, and that airing it is often a solid first step toward a better life. The chapter then links storytelling directly to action from the very beginning.

practice.q: 'The past influences but does not determine the present.' Discuss Egan's guidelines for helping clients talk productively about the past.
practice.answer:
Introduction
Some schools of psychology hold that current problems can only be understood through their historic roots, and they devote much time to the past. Egan accepts that this can work when client and helper agree, but he presents a more action-oriented view and offers guidelines for productive past-talk.

The case against searching for causes
Glasser (2000) argued that people are not victims of their past unless they choose to be, and that the past helps mainly when it focuses on successes. Fish (1995) suggested searching for hidden root causes may be unnecessary, misguided or counterproductive. Deutsch (1954) noted that even in controlled labs causation between successive events is hard to establish, so linking complex present behaviour to complex past events is frustrating. Egan gives three reasons such searches may be futile: causal links remain hypothetical; there is little evidence that understanding the past changes present behaviour; and past-talk focuses on what happened to clients rather than what they did about it, undermining the bias toward action.

The past still matters
The past influences behaviour, and being stuck in it often reflects rejection and resentment. But influence is not determination. Kagan (1996) challenged the "scarred for life" assumption, pointing to concentration-camp orphans and war-displaced children who adapted well.

Three productive uses
First, talk about the past to make sense of the present. How the past is discussed matters more than whether. A man saw his late father's cruel style living on in him in smaller ways; the helper's question "now what?" turned insight toward change. Whether the father caused it is irrelevant, and blaming the past could create a new problem; problems are often bad habits (Duhigg) rather than determinism.

Second, talk about the past to be reconciled to or liberated from it. Clients may reason that they cannot change because their past cannot change; helpers help them challenge this. A father who disclosed his own childhood abuse felt he had thrown off a dirty cloak of shame, which is liberation talk. Helpers should know whether they aim to learn from or be liberated from the past, and not expect a silver bullet. King and Hicks (2007) showed reviewing regrets can foster growth and even gratitude for loss.

Third, talk about the past to prepare for future action. Toynbee said history not used is nothing. Christopher, recognising how he had been made to feel inadequate, resolved not to demean others.

Caveats
These guidelines are not set in stone. Short (2006) listens to past stories with respect so people do not suffer alone; Hansen (2005) warns against devaluing inner experience. Some approaches require deep exploration of the past, and any solid approach can work in competent hands.

Conclusion
For Egan, helping is about the future. The past is worth discussing when it illuminates the present, frees the client, or fuels action, and always with respect for the client's experience.

practice.q: Explain how counsellors can help clients move into action right from the beginning of helping.
practice.answer:
Introduction
A central theme of Egan's book is that helping must not "lose the name of action", in Hamlet's phrase. Clients often fail to manage problems because they do not act intelligently, forcefully and prudently in their own interests. Positive psychology's focus on personal agency and self-regulation (Bandura; Caprara & Cervone) supports this "bias toward action".

Linking Stage I to action
Action should start early, as early gains signal successful therapy. What clients learn in Tasks A, B and C should be linked to the Action Arrow. Sal, a burn patient, needed "engagement" (Auerbach, Salick & Fine). With no grand plan, he talked to a recovered patient, asked for another visit and reached out, small actions that began a flow.

Helping clients be proactive
Inactivity harms body, mind and spirit. A workplace counsellor, using a people-in-systems approach, worked with management, unions and doctors to create light jobs for injured workers who otherwise deteriorated at home; they felt better and the company benefited. Marcus, facing forced retirement, cancer and family crises, decided to take charge with help from his sister-in-law Sarah and friend Sam. He researched his illness, partnered with his doctors, made a living will and pursued neglected interests. Refusing to be a victim, he lived until he died.

Using time between sessions
Especially in short-term helping, helpers should leverage sessions to influence what clients do between them. Wosket reviews each session, asks what the client could do before the next and follows up nonjudgmentally. Sixty-eight percent of psychologists frequently use between-session assignments (Kazantzis et al.). Daitch makes homework part of the contract, citing research linking homework willingness to success; Mahrer reviewed methods; Broder offers techniques, addresses resistance and, with Albert Ellis, developed audiotapes.

Homework: principle over label
The term "homework" can put clients off or feel teacherish. The principle is what matters: use every stage and task as a stimulus for problem-managing and opportunity-developing action, and never assign tasks routinely without a clear purpose. Action can also be spontaneous: Mildred's counsellor bluntly challenged her to seize life again, and she came back with options for finding community.

Box 9.2
The Stage I guidelines include helping clients develop an action orientation, spot early opportunities to change self-defeating behaviour and use innovative homework.

Conclusion
For Egan, action is not something saved for the end of helping. From the first session, helpers link what clients are learning to concrete steps, however small, help them stay active rather than passive, and use the time between sessions to extend the work of each session. Whether through formal homework or spontaneous, organic invitations, the helper's role is to be a catalyst for client action.

practice.q: Write a short note on helping clients clarify key issues and discuss the context of their concerns.
practice.answer:
To clarify means discussing problems and opportunities, including goals, strategies, plans, implementation and feelings, as concretely as possible. Vagueness leads nowhere; clarity moves clients from the general to specific experiences, thoughts, behaviours, intentions, views and decisions. Janice, whose husband is depressed, first says her social life is "a bit restricted"; through empathic highlights and probes it becomes a story of isolation, emotional swings, sleeplessness, self-blame and hidden loneliness. Her own actions, staying home and covering up, are part of the problem. A law student with bulimia who acted "a little erratically" revealed fantasies, purging and rudeness; once her story became public with her helper, she began regaining control.

Discussing context applies the people-in-systems approach. Tarik's complaint of overwork and an undermining subordinate looked routine, but his Canadian counsellor explored his culture and background, learning that Tarik was a new partner given poor clients in a hierarchical culture, with a distant boss and a resentful rival partner. Egan cautions that background should not be sought for its own sake; the right kind and amount provides richness and context. Both guidelines serve the same purpose: turning a vague or routine-sounding story into one concrete enough to act on.

summary: Stage I has three intermingled tasks: help clients tell their story (I-A), find the real story through new perspectives (I-B) and choose the right story to work on (I-C).
Stage I tasks pervade helping: stories leak out over time, new perspectives are always needed, and 'right' means right for the client.
Stage I can be seen as client-focused assessment, a collaborative learning process rather than testing or diagnosis.
Action should be linked to helping from the start; Sal shows small actions can begin a flow without grand plans.

Client self-disclosure is linked to well-being (Sloan), is valuable in itself (Pennebaker) and is usually experienced positively (Farber et al.), though fear of disclosure keeps some away from therapy (Vogel & Wester).
Hanna's precursors of change (necessity, anxiety tolerance, awareness, desire to confront, effort, hope, social support) act as regulators of change.
Clients tell stories in very different styles (Martina vs Nick); helpers adapt while building a working relationship.
Clients may start at any stage of the helping process; helpers join them there.
Severity is subjective as well as objective; Mehrabian & Reed's formula multiplies distress, uncontrollability and frequency; risk and limits of helping must be assessed continuously.
Clarifying moves clients from vague generalities to specifics, and exploring context adds richness (Janice, Tarik).
Searching for past causes is often futile, but the past can be discussed productively to make sense of the present, gain liberation, or prepare for action.
Most clients have unused opportunities and resources; skilled helpers adopt a resource-oriented mind-set and help clients see the opportunity in every problem.
Helping must move into action from the beginning: being proactive and using between-session time productively, with or without the label 'homework'.
